G3A01: More sunspots mean more solar ultraviolet, which ionizes the upper atmosphere more heavily and lets the ionosphere refract higher frequencies, so the upper HF bands open more often. A zero count does not mean no propagation at all; the lower bands still work.
G3A02: A sudden ionospheric disturbance is a burst of X-rays from a solar flare that ionizes the D region on the sunlit side of Earth. The D region absorbs lower frequencies most, so those are hit harder than higher ones, and the dark side is not affected.
G3A03: Ultraviolet and X-rays travel at the speed of light, and light takes about 8 minutes to cover the 150 million km from the Sun to Earth. Slower charged particles from the same event take hours to days.
G3A04: The highest HF bands, 15, 12 and 10 meters, need a strongly ionized F region to refract them, which happens mostly when solar activity is high. At solar minimum the MUF often stays below them, so they are the least reliable for long distance.
G3A05: The solar flux index is the Sun's radio noise measured at a wavelength of 10.7 cm (2800 MHz), a daily measure of solar activity that tracks sunspot numbers closely. It is not a count of sunspots and it is not the MUF.
G3A06: A geomagnetic storm is a temporary disturbance of Earth's magnetic field, usually caused by a burst of charged particles from the Sun such as a coronal mass ejection. It is not a weather thunderstorm or a drop in solar flux.
G3A07: Twenty meters is high enough to escape most daytime absorption yet low enough to be refracted even when the Sun is quiet, so it usually supports worldwide daytime contacts at any point in the solar cycle, not only at the maximum.
G3A08: A geomagnetic storm pours energy into the polar ionosphere, causing heavy absorption and disturbance there, so HF paths through high latitudes are degraded. Ground wave propagation is not affected.
G3A09: High geomagnetic activity produces auroras, and the ionized auroral curtain can reflect VHF signals, allowing unusual contacts on 6 and 2 meters. It does not strengthen HF signals crossing the polar regions; those usually get worse.
G3A10: The Sun rotates about once every 27 days as seen from Earth, so an active region or coronal hole that affects propagation tends to face Earth again about 26 to 28 days later. The Moon's position has nothing to do with it.
G3A11: A coronal mass ejection is a cloud of charged particles moving far slower than light, so it reaches Earth about 15 hours to several days after leaving the Sun. The 8 minute figure applies only to light, ultraviolet and X-rays.
G3A12: The K-index is measured every 3 hours and shows how disturbed Earth's geomagnetic field is in the short term, from 0 (quiet) to 9 (severe storm). It says nothing about the Sun's own magnetic field or sunspot positions.
G3A13: The A-index is a daily average derived from the K-index readings, so it describes the longer-term stability of Earth's geomagnetic field. A low A-index means a quiet field and usually better HF conditions.
G3A14: Coronal holes send out fast streams of charged particles that disturb Earth's magnetic field and ionosphere, which degrades HF communication. VHF and UHF ducting depends on lower-atmosphere weather, not solar particles.
G3B01: The long-path signal travels much farther around the Earth than the short-path one, so it arrives a fraction of a second later and can be heard as a slight echo. It does not produce a steady 3 dB gain or regular fading.
G3B02: All listed items are true. The MUF changes with path distance and location, with time of day and season, and with solar radiation and ionospheric disturbances, since each of these affects how strongly ionized the refracting layer is.
G3B03: Ionospheric absorption falls as frequency rises, so the frequency just below the MUF is attenuated least while still being refracted back to Earth. Frequencies just above the LUF are close to being absorbed outright.
G3B04: Automated receiving networks such as the Reverse Beacon Network or PSK Reporter show where your signal is being heard right now, a direct check of current propagation. The A-index only describes geomagnetic conditions in general.
G3B05: Between the LUF and the MUF a signal is high enough in frequency to avoid being absorbed but low enough to be refracted, so it bends back to Earth and makes skywave contact possible. Above the MUF it would pass through the ionosphere.
G3B06: Below the LUF, absorption in the lower ionosphere, mainly the D region, weakens the signal so much that it is lost before reaching the destination. Passing through the ionosphere is what happens above the MUF.
G3B07: LUF means Lowest Usable Frequency, the lowest frequency that will support communication between two specific points; below it absorption is too great. Like the MUF, it applies to a particular path, not to any point or time window.
G3B08: MUF means Maximum Usable Frequency, the highest frequency that will be refracted back to Earth between two particular points. Frequencies above it pass through the ionosphere and are lost to space for that path.
G3B09: The F2 region is the highest ionospheric layer, roughly 300 km up, so a single hop from it can cover about 2,500 miles along the surface. A hop off the lower E region covers only about 1,200 miles.
G3B10: The E region sits about 100 km up, much lower than the F2 region, so the farthest a single hop from it can reach is about 1,200 miles. The longer 2,500 mile figure belongs to the higher F2 region.
G3B11: When the LUF is higher than the MUF, any frequency low enough to be refracted is also absorbed, so no frequency works and ordinary skywave communication over that path is not possible. Nothing is enhanced.
G3B12: In summer, thunderstorms produce lots of static, and it travels a long way on the lower HF bands such as 80 and 160 meters, so high atmospheric noise is typical there. Those bands do not give worldwide daylight propagation.
G3C01: The D region is the lowest layer of the ionosphere, roughly 60 to 90 km up, below the E region and the F1 and F2 regions. It exists mainly in daylight and absorbs lower HF signals.
G3C02: The critical frequency is the highest frequency that the ionosphere will refract back to Earth at a given angle of incidence; anything higher passes through. It is not defined by signal-to-noise ratio.
G3C03: The F2 region is the highest ionospheric layer, so a wave refracted from it comes down much farther away than one from the lower E region. Its height, not its density or the Doppler effect, gives the longer skip.
G3C04: The critical angle is the highest takeoff angle at which a wave will still be returned to Earth under the conditions of the moment; waves sent more steeply escape through the ionosphere. It is not an azimuth.
G3C05: In daylight the D region forms and absorbs signals on the lower HF bands, so 160, 80, 60 and 40 meters are hard to use for long distance during the day. The F region refracts signals rather than absorbing them.
G3C06: HF scatter signals arrive by many slightly different paths that keep changing, which gives them a characteristic fluttery or hollow sound. Phone signals heard this way usually have poor intelligibility, not high.
G3C07: Scatter signals reach the skip zone by several different paths at once, each with its own length and delay, and the mix of them distorts the sound. Ground wave absorption is not the cause.
G3C08: Only a small fraction of the transmitted energy is scattered back toward the skip zone, so scatter signals there are usually weak. The scattering happens in the ionosphere and at the ground, not in the magnetosphere.
G3C09: Scatter from irregularities in the ionosphere and from the ground sends a little energy into the skip zone, so stations there can be heard faintly. Faraday rotation is a change in polarization, not a way into the skip zone.
G3C10: NVIS sends MF or HF signals almost straight up at high elevation angles so the ionosphere returns them over a nearby area, filling the skip zone out to a few hundred miles. It is used on low bands such as 80 and 40 meters, well below the MUF.
G3C11: The D region is the most absorbent layer for signals below about 10 MHz in daylight, which is why the low bands are weak for long distance by day. The F1 and F2 regions refract rather than absorb.
G4A01: A notch filter removes a very narrow slice of the receiver passband, so it can take out a steady carrier or heterodyne whistle without much harm to the wanted signal. It does nothing to the transmitted bandwidth.
G4A02: Switching to the opposite sideband when receiving CW moves interfering signals to different audio pitches or out of the passband altogether, which may reduce or remove the interference. It has no effect on impulse noise.
G4A03: A noise blanker senses short, sharp pulses such as ignition noise and briefly cuts the receiver gain while each pulse lasts, so the pulse is mostly silenced. It does not simply clip the peaks or widen the bandwidth.
G4A04: With a vacuum tube amplifier, the TUNE control brings the plate circuit to resonance, and at resonance the plate current falls to a pronounced dip. A peak would mean the circuit is off resonance.
G4A05: ALC feeds back a voltage that lowers the drive when it would push the amplifier too hard, preventing excessive drive and the distortion and splatter it causes. It is not there to balance audio response.
G4A06: An antenna tuner matches the transmitter to the impedance seen at its end of the feed line, so more power is transferred from the transmitter into the line. It does not lower the SWR or the losses on the feed line itself.
G4A07: Noise reduction (DSP) works by processing the received audio, and the harder it is set, the more it can affect the wanted signal too, so signals may sound distorted or watery. It does not shift or destabilize the frequency.
G4A08: The LOAD or COUPLING control is set to get the desired power output without going over the tube's maximum allowable plate current. Minimum SWR at the antenna is set by the antenna system, not by this control.
G4A09: The external amplifier needs a few milliseconds after keying to switch its relays and connect the antenna to its output; delaying RF avoids sending power into open or switching contacts. It is not about key clicks.
G4A10: An electronic keyer automatically forms dots and dashes of correct length and spacing from a paddle, making CW sending easier and more even. Transmit and receive switching is done by other circuits.
G4A11: AFSK data modes need a clean, linear signal, and ALC action changes the gain unevenly and distorts it, causing splatter and errors. Drive is set by audio level so ALC stays inactive; ALC does not invert the modulation.
G4A12: Dual VFOs let you transmit on one frequency and listen on another, which is how split operation works, for example with DX stations. They do not let you transmit on two frequencies or work full duplex.
G4A13: A receive attenuator lowers incoming signal levels before the receiver front end, preventing overload when very strong signals are present. It has no effect on transmit power or on audio volume.
G4B01: An oscilloscope has a vertical amplifier for the signal being measured and a horizontal amplifier for the sweep or second input, so it can draw a graph of the waveform. Ohmmeters, signal generators and ammeters have none.
G4B02: An oscilloscope shows the waveform itself, so it can display and measure complex waveforms that a digital voltmeter would reduce to one number. It is not generally more precise, and it uses more power.
G4B03: An oscilloscope shows the actual shape of each CW keyed element, so you can see whether the rise and fall are smooth or so sharp that they cause key clicks. A wavemeter only indicates frequency.
G4B04: To see the RF envelope, a sample of the transmitter's actual output, reduced to a safe level by an attenuator, goes to the vertical input. The local oscillator or mixer output would not show what is actually being transmitted.
G4B05: A meter with high input impedance draws very little current from the circuit, so it disturbs the circuit less and reads its true voltage more accurately. It does not let a meter measure higher voltages safely.
G4B06: A digital multimeter shows a numeric reading with more significant digits than you can read off an analog pointer, so it offers higher precision. Its response is not faster, which is why analog meters are still used for tuning.
G4B07: A two-tone test feeds two audio tones that are not harmonically related into an SSB transmitter. Unrelated tones make any intermodulation products easy to spot on a spectrum display and give a steady envelope to check.
G4B08: A two-tone test shows the linearity of a transmitter or amplifier: a linear one reproduces the two tones without extra intermodulation products or a flattened envelope. Carrier suppression is measured with other tests.
G4B09: An analog meter's moving pointer makes it easy to see a peak or dip while adjusting a circuit for maximum or minimum, where a digital display's changing digits are hard to follow. Digital meters are better for precision.
G4B10: A directional wattmeter measures forward and reflected power separately, and from those two readings you can work out the standing wave ratio. It cannot tell you an antenna's front-to-back ratio or propagation.
G4B11: An antenna analyzer contains its own low-power signal source, so for an SWR check you connect it to the antenna and its feed line. Neither the transmitter nor a receiver is connected.
G4B12: An antenna analyzer works with very low power, so strong signals picked up from nearby transmitters add received power at its input and throw off its SWR readings. It does not generate harmonics from them.
G4B13: An antenna analyzer measures impedance, SWR and related values at its connector, so it can measure the impedance of coaxial cable, for example characteristic impedance with the far end terminated. It cannot measure antenna gain or transmitter output.
G4C01: A bypass capacitor offers a low impedance path to ground for RF while leaving audio almost untouched, so it diverts RF out of audio circuits. An inductor would do the opposite, passing low frequencies and blocking RF.
G4C02: Arcing at a poor electrical connection creates sharp, irregular sparks that produce noise across a very wide range of frequencies. Missing or misused baluns cause feed line problems, not broadband noise.
G4C03: When an audio device picks up RF from an SSB phone transmitter, it detects the varying envelope and you hear distorted speech. A clean, clearly audible voice is unlikely because the device is not a proper SSB detector.
G4C04: A CW transmitter turns its carrier on and off, and a device rectifying that RF produces on-and-off humming or clicking in time with the keying. You will not hear a clean CW tone, because there is no beat oscillator.
G4C05: If the ground wire happens to have a high impedance at the operating frequency, for example because its length is near a quarter wavelength, high RF voltages appear at the equipment end and can cause RF burns. Insulated wire or braid does not cause this.
G4C06: A ground wire that is resonant, such as a quarter wavelength long, presents a high impedance at the station end, so high RF voltages can appear on the equipment enclosures. It does not make ground straps overheat or rods corrode.
G4C07: A lightning strike carries a huge current that heats the connection, and solder melts at a low temperature, so a soldered joint will likely be destroyed. Clamped or welded connections are used instead.
G4C08: A ferrite choke on the cable adds high impedance to common-mode RF current flowing on the outside of the cable, reducing the interference without affecting the audio. Shorting or grounding the center conductor would kill the audio.
G4C09: Bonding all equipment enclosures together with short, heavy conductors keeps them at the same potential, so less current flows between them through cable shields and ground loops are minimized. Connecting grounds in series makes things worse.
G4C10: A ground loop in audio connections lets AC-related current flow in cable shields, which adds hum to the audio and therefore to your transmitted signal. It does not change the antenna SWR.
G4C11: Bonding all equipment enclosures together keeps them at one RF potential, so there are fewer points where RF voltage builds up and causes hot spots. Surge suppressor outlets protect against power surges, not RF.
G4C12: Grounding a metal enclosure means that if a live wire touches it, the current flows to ground and trips a breaker or fuse instead of leaving a dangerous voltage on the chassis. It does not prevent a fuse from blowing.
G4D01: A speech processor raises the average level of the voice relative to its peaks, so transmitted speech sounds louder and punches through better. It does not prevent distortion; set too high it causes it.
G4D02: A speech processor compresses or clips the voice so the quieter parts are brought up, raising average power while peak power stays the same. It does not increase peak power or reduce distortion.
G4D03: All listed items are true. Too much speech processing gives distorted speech, extra intermodulation products that can splatter onto nearby frequencies, and more background noise brought up along with the voice.
G4D04: An S meter shows the strength of the received signal in S units, with each unit about 6 dB. It does not measure transmitter output or impedance.
G4D05: Twenty dB is a power ratio of 10 to the power of 2, or 100, so a signal 20 dB over S9 is 100 times more powerful than one at S9. A ratio of 20 times would be only about 13 dB.
G4D06: On a calibrated S meter each S unit stands for about 6 dB, a fourfold change in power. That is why a move from S8 to S9 takes about four times the power.
G4D07: One S unit is about 6 dB, and 6 dB is a power ratio of about 4, so the transmitter power must go up about four times to raise the reading from S8 to S9. Doubling power gives only 3 dB, half an S unit.
G4D08: Lower sideband sits below the displayed carrier frequency, so a 3 kHz LSB signal set at 7.178 MHz occupies 7.175 to 7.178 MHz. The range 7.178 to 7.181 MHz would be upper sideband.
G4D09: Upper sideband sits above the displayed carrier frequency, so a 3 kHz USB signal set at 14.347 MHz occupies 14.347 to 14.350 MHz. The range 14.344 to 14.347 MHz would be lower sideband.
G4D10: LSB extends about 3 kHz below the displayed carrier frequency, so the carrier must be at least 3 kHz above the lower edge of the phone segment to keep the whole signal inside it. A 1 kHz margin would let 2 kHz spill out.
G4D11: USB extends about 3 kHz above the displayed carrier frequency, so the carrier must be at least 3 kHz below the upper edge of the band to keep the whole signal inside it. Setting it above the edge would put you out of band.
G4E01: A capacitance hat is a set of spokes or a disk near the top of a short mobile whip that adds capacitance, making the antenna act electrically longer so it resonates lower with less loading coil. It does not raise power handling.
G4E02: A corona ball is a smooth ball on the tip of an HF mobile antenna; it spreads out the high RF voltage at the tip so less corona discharge occurs while transmitting. It is not a bumper against striking objects.
G4E03: A 100-watt HF rig draws around 20 amps, so it should be wired directly to the battery with heavy-gauge wire, fused, to keep voltage drop low. The alternator is not a stable connection point, and transmission line is not power wire.
G4E04: Auxiliary power sockets are usually wired and fused for only about 10 to 15 amps, while a 100-watt transceiver can draw 20 amps or more on transmit, so the wiring may be inadequate. Polarity is the same as the radio's.
G4E05: An HF mobile antenna is usually much shorter than a quarter wavelength, so it has low radiation resistance and loses much of its power in loading coils and ground losses. That inefficiency limits a mobile station far more than wire gauge does.
G4E06: A shortened, loaded mobile antenna has a high Q, so it stays well matched over only a narrow range of frequencies and must often be retuned. Its Q is high, not very low.
G4E07: All listed items are true. A vehicle's battery charging system, fuel delivery system such as the fuel pump, and control computers can all produce electrical noise that interferes with HF reception.
G4E08: Solar cells are wired in series to build up voltage and in parallel to build up current, so a panel uses a series-parallel arrangement. Shunt and bypass are not ways of combining the cells.
G4E09: A fully lit silicon photovoltaic cell gives about 0.5 volts with no load, which is why many cells are connected in series to reach a useful voltage. A figure of 1.38 volts is far too high for one silicon cell.
G4E10: When the panel is dark its output voltage drops below the battery's, and current could flow back from the battery through the panel. A series diode blocks that reverse flow. It does not regulate the charging voltage.
G4E11: Lithium iron phosphate batteries need carefully controlled charging voltage and current, so a charge controller suited to that chemistry must sit between the solar panel and the battery. A series resistor cannot do this job.
